I was meeting a friend downtown last Saturday afternoon.
We agreed to meet at a coffee shop at two o'clock.
I left home a little late, so I needed to hurry the whole way.
I used my phone for directions because I didn't know the area very well.
I followed the map carefully, turning left and right through new streets.
Everything was going fine for the first ten minutes.
Then, halfway there, my phone screen suddenly went black.
I pressed the button many times, but nothing happened at all.
My phone had completely died, with no warning at all.
I stood on the street corner, unsure what to do next.
I didn't remember the exact address of the coffee shop.
I only remembered it was somewhere near a big park.
I walked toward the park, hoping to recognize something familiar.
The streets all looked similar, and I started to feel a little lost.
I had no way to call my friend either, which made it worse.
I checked my pockets again, hoping for a spare charger I didn't have.
After walking for ten minutes, I saw a small shop with a sign for phone chargers.
I walked in and asked if I could charge my phone for a few minutes.
The shop owner said yes and pointed to a chair.
I waited there for almost fifteen minutes, watching the little battery symbol slowly fill up.
My phone slowly turned back on, and I felt very relieved.
I quickly opened my messages to check for my friend.
She had sent three messages, all asking where I was.
I called her right away and explained what happened to my phone.
She laughed and said she was still waiting patiently at the coffee shop.
I thanked the shop owner and walked the rest of the way, following the map again.
I arrived only twenty-five minutes late, which felt better than I expected it to feel.
My friend wasn't angry at all about it.
We both agreed that phones die at the worst possible times, always without warning.
She told me a similar story from a few months ago, about a trip to the airport.
It made me feel less alone in my bad luck.
Now, I always carry a small battery pack in my bag, just in case.
It's a small thing, but it has already saved me twice since that day.
One dead phone taught me to always be ready for the unexpected, no matter how careful I usually am.
